prohibited_recommendations: Do not diagnose early Alzheimer's disease from a family history and a cognitive complaint when memory testing is normal and onset was abrupt
Do not attribute an abrupt focal cognitive syndrome to stress or anxiety
Do not start a cholinesterase inhibitor for a strategic infarct syndrome
Do not clear her to return to teaching or to drive without formal assessment of the parietal deficits
required_recommendations: Test parietal functions specifically — finger naming, right-left orientation, written calculation, writing — because the screen does not capture them
Recognise that abrupt onset with no progression over six months is a stroke syndrome, not a degenerative one
Obtain brain MRI: the lesion location explains the syndrome and dates the event
Document normal memory on formal testing, which is what excludes early Alzheimer's disease here
Institute secondary prevention after a documented infarct
Address fitness to work and to drive, and answer the family's question about Alzheimer's disease explicitly

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG has no diagnostic role in vascular cognitive impairment; it belongs to the differential of a rapidly progressive or fluctuating course (Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, non-convulsive status, toxic-metabolic encephalopathy), none of which is present here

A presynaptic dopaminergic study answers the Lewy-body question, not the vascular one, and there is no spontaneous parkinsonism, no fluctuating cognition with hallucinations and no REM sleep behaviour disorder
Cardiac sympathetic imaging is a test for dementia with Lewy bodies and for autonomic failure; it says nothing about cerebrovascular disease

An untargeted paraneoplastic or autoimmune-encephalitis battery in a chronic stepwise decline with a hypertensive imaging burden is the archetypal expensive miss; the indication for those assays is a subacute multidomain syndrome
The MRI already obtained answers everything a CT could and more: CT cannot show microbleeds or cortical superficial siderosis, so it cannot grade the vascular burden this diagnosis rests on
There is no embolic lesion pattern to explain: the burden here is small-vessel, and a structural cardioembolic source would not account for it
Prolonged rhythm monitoring is for an unexplained embolic infarct pattern; in pure small-vessel disease it changes nothing about the diagnosis or the treatment

accepted: Vascular dementia — strategic single-infarct type, left angular gyrus infarct producing Gerstmann's syndrome with loss of occupational function

differential.key_features: The family history and the patient's own conviction make this the presumptive diagnosis on referral, but memory is normal on formal testing, the hippocampi show no atrophy, the onset was abrupt over one afternoon and there has been no progression in six months
A parietal presentation in a younger patient, but it is insidious and progressive with bilateral parieto-occipital atrophy, none of which is present here

differential.diagnosis: Transient ischaemic attack with functional overlay
differential.key_features: The deficits are objectively present six months later and anatomically coherent with a demonstrated infarct
The initial attribution to stress; but finger agnosia and right-left disorientation are not produced by anxiety, and the infarct is visible
Naming, fluency and repetition are intact and the syndrome is parietal rather than linguistic

key_clinical_evidence: The Gerstmann tetrad localises: finger agnosia, right-left disorientation, dysgraphia and dyscalculia together point to the left angular gyrus, and a lesion there was found
In early Alzheimer's disease delayed recall is the first domain to fail; normal free recall and recognition with a severe parietal syndrome is the wrong shape for it
Abrupt onset in one afternoon with six months of stability is the temporal signature of an infarct, and the family history is the reason the temporal signature was ignored
A cognitive syndrome can cost a patient her occupation without touching her memory, and the assessment must therefore be functional as well as diagnostic
The absence of medial temporal atrophy in a 64-year-old with cognitive complaints is a strong negative for Alzheimer's disease and can be obtained from the same MRI that shows the infarct

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Silvia Donati is a 64-year-old primary school teacher who attends with her husband, convinced she has early Alzheimer's disease because her mother was diagnosed at 72. Six months ago, over a single afternoon, she found she could not write the class register or add up marks; the episode lasted several hours and her general practitioner attributed it to stress. She returned to work but has not been able to teach since: she cannot mark arithmetic, mixes up left and right when directing children, and makes letter errors when writing on the board. She has been on sick leave for four months. Her husband adds that she loses her place when reading and has twice missed a turning on the left while driving. Her memory for events and conversations is, in his account, essentially normal — she runs the household diary and has not missed an appointment. The change was abrupt and dates to that afternoon; there has been no progression over six months. She has hypertension treated for eight years and takes a statin. There are no hallucinations, no fluctuation and no dream enactment. She is anxious about the diagnosis and asks directly whether she has her mother's disease.

neurological_exam.additional: Finger agnosia, right-left disorientation, dysgraphia and dyscalculia together — the four elements of Gerstmann's syndrome. Pulse regular at 68.
neurological_exam.coordination: Intact. Ideomotor praxis intact to command.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal and reactive. Extraocular movements full. Visual fields full to confrontation on repeated testing. Face symmetric. Speech fluent without paraphasia.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and fully oriented. MoCA 22/30. The pattern is unusual: she loses points on the cube, the clock, serial sevens and delayed recall, but on focused testing she cannot name her own fingers on either hand, cannot distinguish right from left reliably, cannot perform written calculation beyond single digits, and writes with letter omissions and reversals. Naming of objects is intact; reading aloud is intact for words but she loses her place in a line of text.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk, tone and strength. No drift, no tremor.
neurological_exam.sensory: Intact to primary modalities. Graphaesthesia impaired in the right hand.
